unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brackenbury Fashions Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 46 staff across 3 high-street stores, selling mid-priced womenswear. Last year Country X's economy shrank by 2.1%, unemployment rose from 5.2% to 8.6% and the consumer confidence index fell from 105 to 78. Brackenbury's annual sales dropped 18% to $1.86 million as fewer shoppers entered its stores and average basket values fell. Footfall fell 22% over the same 12 months.

The directors are choosing between launching a budget 'Essentials' range priced 30% below current lines to win cautious shoppers, or holding prices and trimming 8 staff through redundancy to protect margins. Two discounter competitors have already opened near Brackenbury's stores this year. The range would be ready for the spring season in 4 months. The board meets next week to decide.

questions.question_text: Define 'recession'.
questions.model_answer: A period of at least two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, when economic output and spending decline [2].

knowledge_max_2: falling GDP for two or more consecutive quarters
a period of declining economic activity and output

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Brackenbury's sales fell when Country X's economy shrank.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rising unemployment reduces household disposable income [k], so fewer shoppers can afford mid-priced womenswear, and annual sales dropped 18% to $1.86 million [app]. Reason 2: Falling consumer confidence makes people delay non-essential purchases [k], and with the confidence index down from 105 to 78, shoppers cut basket values and footfall fell 22% [app].

knowledge_max_2: unemployment reduces disposable income and spending power
falling consumer confidence makes households delay non-essential purchases
application_max_2: sales dropped 18% to $1.86 million at the 3 high-street stores
confidence index fell from 105 to 78 and footfall fell 22%

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Brackenbury of launching the budget 'Essentials' range.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A budget range widens the customer base [k], letting Brackenbury attract shoppers who abandoned mid-priced lines as unemployment rose to 8.6% and confidence fell to 78 [app], so lost footfall could be recovered [an]. Benefit 2: Lower-priced volume raises sales per store [k], and priced 30% below current lines the range could win back the 22% footfall lost this year [app], so capacity at the 3 high-street stores is better used [an].

knowledge_max_2: a budget range attracts price-sensitive customers and widens the customer base
lower prices can lift sales volume and capacity use
application_max_2: unemployment rose to 8.6% and confidence fell to 78, so shoppers traded down
Essentials priced 30% below current lines targets the 22% footfall lost
analysis_max_2: recovering lost footfall restores revenue towards previous levels
higher volume per store improves capacity utilisation and spreads fixed costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenbury Fashions should launch the 'Essentials' range rather than trim 8 staff through redundancy? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Launching Essentials would rebuild demand among cautious shoppers [k]; the range is priced 30% below current lines and arrives in 4 months, directly targeting the customers who disappeared as unemployment rose from 5.2% to 8.6% and confidence fell from 105 to 78 [app], so revenue could recover towards $1.86 million and beyond without cutting the 46 staff who drive sales [an]. However, trimming 8 staff to 38 would cut wage costs quickly [k]; with sales already down 18%, leaner staffing protects margins if the Essentials range cannibalises existing mid-priced lines instead of adding new shoppers [app], so the redundancy option limits losses if the recovery fails to arrive [an]. Overall, Brackenbury should launch Essentials [eval], because redundancy saves wages once but risks lasting damage to service and morale at the 3 high-street stores, while a budget range answers falling consumer confidence of 78 and could recover the 22% footfall lost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a budget range targets price-sensitive shoppers when confidence falls
redundancy cuts wage costs quickly but removes capacity and can harm morale
application_max_2: Essentials priced 30% below current lines, ready in 4 months, targets the post-2.1%-shrinkage market
sales already down 18% to $1.86 million; 8 staff cut to 38 protects margins
analysis_max_2: range option recovers revenue but risks cannibalising mid-priced lines
redundancy option limits losses but weakens the ability to serve recovering demand
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the confidence index of 78 and the 22% footfall loss
recommendation consistent with protecting long-term brand strength over short-term cost cuts

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Callowmere Supermarkets is a private limited company in Country X, operating 9 stores and employing 320 staff. Country X's inflation rate climbed from 6.1% to 11.3% over the past year, and food prices have risen 14% while average wages have grown only 6%. Callowmere's sales revenue rose 9% to $48.5 million, but the number of items sold fell 4%, and shoppers are switching from branded goods to own-label lines. Own-label now reaches 44% of basket value.

The managing director must decide whether to hold own-label prices and absorb supplier cost increases, squeezing margins, or to raise prices across the board by 8% and risk shoppers defecting to discounters. Two rival discounters opened within 5 km of the busiest store this year. Margins on branded grocery lines are already thin. The decision is needed before the autumn supplier review in 6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'inflation'.
questions.model_answer: A sustained general rise in the price level of goods and services in an economy over time [2].

knowledge_max_2: a sustained rise in the general price level
prices of goods and services increase over time

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of rising inflation on Callowmere Supermarkets.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Supplier costs rise faster than wages [k], and with food prices up 14% against only 6% wage growth, Callowmere's shelf prices squeeze shoppers' real incomes [app]. Effect 2: Shoppers switch to cheaper alternatives [k], which is why the number of items sold fell 4% and own-label lines now reach 44% of basket value [app].

knowledge_max_2: inflation raises input and stock costs faster than wages
inflation reduces consumers' real purchasing power and shifts demand to cheaper goods
application_max_2: food prices rose 14% while average wages grew only 6%
items sold fell 4% and own-label basket share reached 44%

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Callowmere of raising prices across the board by 8%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Higher shelf prices accelerate shopper defections [k], and two rival discounters already opened within 5 km of the busiest store this year, so an 8% rise could push price-sensitive families to rivals [app], cutting sales volume further [an]. Problem 2: Raising prices when real wages grew only 6% outstrips pay rises [k], and shoppers already cut items purchased by 4% as inflation hit 11.3% [app], so basket values could shrink despite the 8% rise [an].

knowledge_max_2: price rises can drive customers to cheaper competitors
price rises exceeding income growth shrink real demand
application_max_2: two discounters opened within 5 km of the busiest store; Callowmere plans an 8% rise
items sold already fell 4% with inflation at 11.3% and wages up only 6%
analysis_max_2: lost volume to discounters compounds the 4% decline already seen
revenue may fail to cover the supplier cost increases the rise is meant to offset

questions.question_text: Do you think Callowmere Supermarkets should hold own-label prices rather than raise prices across the board by 8%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Holding own-label prices defends Callowmere's value position [k]; with own-label at 44% of basket value and inflation at 11.3%, keeping these prices steady protects the shoppers most squeezed by the gap between 14% food inflation and 6% wage growth [app], so footfall and loyalty should hold even if own-label margins turn negative short term [an]. However, holding prices means absorbing supplier increases [k]; with revenue of $48.5 million up 9% only because of price rises, flat own-label prices could erase profit on high-volume lines just as two new discounters open within 5 km [app], so the board would need to fund the gap from higher-margin branded lines [an]. Overall, Callowmere should hold own-label prices [eval], because an across-the-board 8% rise clashes with items already falling 4%, while targeted rises on branded goods can recover margin without driving away the value shoppers Callowmere needs [eval].

knowledge_max_2: holding value prices protects price-sensitive customers during inflation
absorbing supplier rises squeezes margins when input costs outpace wages
application_max_2: own-label at 44% of basket value; inflation 11.3% vs wage growth of 6%
$48.5 million revenue up 9% on price rises; two discounters within 5 km
analysis_max_2: loyalty and footfall protection versus margin erosion on own-label lines
risk of losing volume to discounters if all prices rise 8%
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to the 4% decline in items sold
recommendation weighs targeted branded rises against across-the-board increases

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Pennyroyal Café is an independent café in Country X employing 14 staff and serving breakfast, brunch and lunch, founded 5 years ago. Country X's GDP grew by 4.2% last year, unemployment fell to 3.8% and restaurant spending has risen 11% over 2 years. Pennyroyal's monthly revenue reached $86,000, up from $61,000 two years ago, and weekend waiting times now average 25 minutes. Consumer confidence is at its highest for a decade.

The owners are deciding whether to open a second café in the retail park 3 km away, costing $240,000, or to extend the current site by refitting 40 seats and keeping one location. The new site could seat 55 customers and serve a growing industrial estate. The expansion decision must be made before the retail park lease is allocated in 8 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'economic growth'.
questions.model_answer: An increase in the value of goods and services produced in an economy, measured by the rise in GDP [2].

knowledge_max_2: an increase in real GDP / output of goods and services
the economy produces more value over time

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Pennyroyal's revenue grew during the economic boom.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rising GDP lifts household incomes [k], and with unemployment down to 3.8% and GDP up 4.2%, more customers treat café meals as everyday spending rather than a luxury [app]. Reason 2: Strong consumer confidence encourages spending on leisure [k], and with restaurant spending up 11% over 2 years, Pennyroyal's monthly revenue rose from $61,000 to $86,000 [app].

knowledge_max_2: economic growth raises household incomes and purchasing power
consumer confidence rises in a boom, boosting discretionary spending
application_max_2: GDP grew 4.2% and unemployment fell to 3.8%
restaurant spending rose 11% and monthly revenue climbed from $61,000 to $86,000

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Pennyroyal of opening the retail park café.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A second site widens the catchment [k], tapping the growing industrial estate and retail park trade instead of only the current street [app], so total revenue could rise beyond $86,000 a month [an]. Benefit 2: Two venues share customer goodwill and catering costs [k], and with 55 customers seated the $240,000 build cost can be spread across higher combined volume [app], improving overall profit margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: a new location reaches new customers and widens the catchment
expansion spreads fixed costs and shared resources across sites
application_max_2: retail park near a growing industrial estate, 3 km from the current site
new site seating 55 customers for $240,000 versus refitting 40 seats
analysis_max_2: higher combined volume lifts total revenue above $86,000 a month
fixed costs spread over two sites improve margins if demand holds

questions.question_text: Do you think Pennyroyal Café should open the retail park café rather than extend the current site? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Opening the retail park site would capture the boom at its peak [k]; with GDP up 4.2%, unemployment at 3.8% and restaurant spending up 11%, a café seating 55 customers near the industrial estate could reach a new market while the original site keeps the loyal crowd causing 25-minute weekend waits [app], so revenue could grow well past $86,000 a month [an]. However, extending the current site by refitting 40 seats is cheaper and less risky [k]; it costs far less than $240,000 and keeps one 14-person team focused on one location [app], so profit per café rises without duplicated management or split oversight while the boom lasts [an]. Overall, Pennyroyal should open the retail park café [eval], because demand fundamentals (GDP +4.2%, confidence at its highest for a decade) support two locations, and waiting 8 weeks risks losing the lease to a rival [eval].

knowledge_max_2: opening a second site captures new markets during rapid growth
extending the existing site is cheaper and keeps management simple
application_max_2: $240,000 new site seating 55 customers near a growing industrial estate
current site refit of 40 seats; weekend waits of 25 minutes at $86,000 monthly revenue
analysis_max_2: two-site revenue growth and capacity relief versus $240,000 outlay and execution risk
single-site efficiency and lower risk versus missing the retail park lease deadline
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the 8-week lease deadline and boom-stage demand
recommendation links back to confidence at its highest for a decade

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Calder Vale Motors is a franchised car dealership in Country X employing 38 staff at a ring-road site. Country X's economy has contracted for 3 consecutive quarters, unemployment has risen to 9.4% and consumer confidence has fallen to its lowest in 12 years. Car sales at Calder Vale dropped 24% last year to 610 vehicles, and the used-car forecourt is ageing, with 140 cars unsold for over 60 days. New-car showroom visits are down 30% year on year.

The dealer principal must choose between a 'Sale Days' promotion offering 8% discounts and free 2-year servicing to clear stock, or cutting forecourt costs by making 5 sales staff redundant and reducing marketing spend by 40%. Rivals have cut prices by up to 10%. The decision is due before quarter end, in 5 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'consumer confidence'.
questions.model_answer: A measure of how optimistic households feel about the economy, influencing their willingness to spend, especially on big-ticket items [2].

knowledge_max_2: a measure of household optimism about the economy
confidence influences willingness to spend, especially on major purchases

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why car sales fell at Calder Vale.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Low consumer confidence makes buyers postpone major purchases [k], and with confidence at its lowest in 12 years, new-car showroom visits fell 30% and sales dropped 24% to 610 vehicles [app]. Reason 2: Rising unemployment reduces disposable income [k], and at 9.4% unemployment many households delay replacing cars, leaving 140 cars unsold for over 60 days [app].

knowledge_max_2: low confidence makes households delay big-ticket purchases
rising unemployment reduces disposable income available for car purchases
application_max_2: confidence at its lowest in 12 years; showroom visits down 30% and sales down 24% to 610
unemployment at 9.4%; 140 used cars unsold for over 60 days

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Calder Vale of making 5 sales staff redundant.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Redundancy cuts sales capacity [k], and with 38 staff already stretched and 610 vehicles to shift, losing 5 experienced salespeople leaves fewer people to close deals [app], so any demand upturn would be harder to capture [an]. Problem 2: Redundancy damages morale among remaining staff [k], leaving 33 employees facing the pressure of clearing 140 aged cars with 9.4% unemployment weighing on buyers [app], so motivation and customer service may decline [an].

knowledge_max_2: redundancies reduce the workforce and sales capacity
redundancy harms morale and service quality among remaining staff
application_max_2: losing 5 of 38 staff leaves 33 to shift 610 vehicles and 140 aged cars
buyers already hesitant at 9.4% unemployment need more, not fewer, sales staff
analysis_max_2: reduced capacity weakens the response when confidence recovers
low morale among 33 remaining staff risks weaker service and lost deals

questions.question_text: Do you think Calder Vale Motors should run the 'Sale Days' promotion rather than make 5 sales staff redundant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The Sale Days promotion attacks the real problem [k]; sales fell 24% to 610 vehicles because confidence is at its lowest in 12 years, so 8% discounts and free 2-year servicing directly lower the cost of buying now [app], which could clear the 140 aged cars and revive showroom footfall [an]. However, redundancy would cut overheads immediately [k]; with marketing spend reduced by 40% and 5 fewer salaries, Calder Vale preserves cash while sales run 24% below last year [app], but it sells into a falling market with a weaker team and 140 cars still ageing on the forecourt [an]. Overall, Calder Vale should run the Sale Days promotion [eval], because the slump is cyclical and confidence can recover, while 140 unsold cars and showroom visits down 30% demand action to move vehicles, not a smaller sales force [eval].

knowledge_max_2: discounting stimulates demand when confidence is low
redundancy cuts fixed labour costs but removes capacity and may harm morale
application_max_2: Sales Days with 8% discounts and free 2-year servicing vs 140 unsold cars
marketing spend cut by 40% and 5 of 38 staff made redundant
analysis_max_2: promotion clears stock and revives footfall versus margin erosion on each deal
redundancy saves cash now but leaves the dealer weak when demand recovers
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation linked to confidence at its lowest in 12 years
recommendation favours revenue action over cost cuts for aged stock

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Rillwater Construction Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 78 construction workers and site managers. Country X's economy grew 3.6% last year, unemployment fell to 4.1% and housebuilding approvals rose 17%. Three new housing estates are due to start this year. Rillwater's order book is worth $9.4 million, its fullest in 6 years, but it has turned down 2 contracts worth $2.8 million because it lacks enough skilled bricklayers and electricians.

Average site wages in the region have risen 12%. The directors are deciding whether to raise wages by 10% across the 78 workers to attract staff from rivals, or to subcontract the 2 new contracts at rates that cut profit margins from 9% to 5%. Subcontractors would demand 25% deposits upfront. The decision is needed before the housing developer signs next month.

questions.question_text: Define 'boom'.
questions.model_answer: A period of rapid economic growth when output, employment and confidence are high [2].

knowledge_max_2: a period of rapid economic growth
high output, high employment and strong demand

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of low unemployment on Rillwater.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Skilled labour becomes scarce [k], and with unemployment at just 4.1% and site wages up 12%, Rillwater turned down 2 contracts worth $2.8 million for lack of bricklayers and electricians [app]. Effect 2: Recruiting from rivals costs more [k], and with GDP growth of 3.6% and three new housing estates due to start, keeping the 78 workers it has is harder [app].

knowledge_max_2: low unemployment creates skills shortages
low unemployment pushes wages up and intensifies competition for staff
application_max_2: unemployment fell to 4.1% and site wages rose 12%
2 contracts worth $2.8 million turned down for lack of skilled trades

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Rillwater of raising wages by 10%.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Higher pay attracts scarce skilled labour [k], letting Rillwater take on the 2 contracts worth $2.8 million instead of losing them again [app], directly lifting revenue and workload [an]. Benefit 2: Better pay improves retention and morale [k], so the 78 workers are less likely to leave for rivals whose site wages already rose 12% [app], protecting site productivity and delivery dates [an].

knowledge_max_2: higher wages attract scarce skilled staff
higher wages improve retention and morale
application_max_2: 10% wage rise targets the 2 contracts worth $2.8 million
78 workers retained against rivals whose wages rose 12%
analysis_max_2: revenue and workload rise when the $2.8 million contracts are won
lower turnover protects productivity and on-time delivery

questions.question_text: Do you think Rillwater Construction should raise wages by 10% rather than subcontract the 2 contracts? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising wages by 10% retains and attracts the skilled trades Rillwater needs [k]; with unemployment at 4.1%, GDP growth of 3.6% and wages already up 12% in the region, higher pay is the realistic way to win the 2 contracts worth $2.8 million while keeping the $9.4 million order book on schedule [app], so revenue and reputation both benefit despite higher payroll costs [an]. However, subcontracting avoids permanent wage inflation [k]; paying 25% deposits upfront and accepting margins cut from 9% to 5% on the 2 contracts would still clear the workload if recruiting fails [app], so subcontracting protects cash while the labour market stays tight [an]. Overall, Rillwater should raise wages by 10% [eval], because subcontracting at 5% margin sacrifices profit on $2.8 million of work, whereas higher wages keep control of quality, schedules and the full 9% margin on the strongest order book in 6 years [eval].

knowledge_max_2: raising wages attracts and retains scarce skilled workers in a boom
subcontracting avoids permanent wage increases but erodes margins
application_max_2: 10% wage rise vs 2 contracts worth $2.8 million and a $9.4 million order book
subcontract margins cut from 9% to 5% with 25% deposits upfront
analysis_max_2: winning the contracts with permanent staff protects quality and schedule control
subcontracting clears workload but halves the margin and demands cash deposits
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the 6-year-high order book of $9.4 million
recommendation weighs long-term capability against short-term cash protection

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Skerry Bay Hotel is a 3-star hotel in Country X with 120 rooms and 64 employees. Country X entered slump last year: GDP fell 1.4%, unemployment reached 10.2% and household spending on holidays fell 16%. Revenue fell from $3.1 million to $2.4 million, occupancy dropped from 71% to 58%, and international tourist numbers fell 9%. Corporate bookings, once 30% of revenue, have dried up completely.

The general manager must decide whether to cut room rates by 15% to appeal to domestic families who can no longer afford overseas holidays, or keep rates unchanged and close the leisure wing, making 9 staff redundant. Rival hotels have already cut rates by 12%. The decision is required before the summer brochure goes to print in 7 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'slump'.
questions.model_answer: The lowest point of the business cycle, when GDP is stagnant or falling, demand is weak and unemployment is high [2].

knowledge_max_2: the lowest point of the business cycle
weak demand, high unemployment and stagnant or falling GDP

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Skerry Bay's occupancy fell during the slump.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher unemployment cuts discretionary travel spending [k], and with unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%, fewer families booked Skerry Bay, dropping occupancy from 71% to 58% [app]. Reason 2: Weak confidence and incomes reduce business tourism [k], and with GDP down 1.4% and corporate bookings dried up completely, international tourist numbers also fell 9% [app].

knowledge_max_2: high unemployment reduces disposable income for leisure travel
weak growth and confidence reduce business and overseas travel
application_max_2: unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%; occupancy fell from 71% to 58%
GDP down 1.4%, corporate bookings dried up completely and international visitors fell 9%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Skerry Bay Hotel of cutting room rates by 15%.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Lower rates attract domestic families trading down from poor value overseas trips [k], directly targeting the 16% drop in overseas holiday spending [app], so occupancy can recover from 58% towards the previous 71% [an]. Benefit 2: Higher occupancy lifts on-site dining and bar revenue [k], and with 120 rooms each night filling at a 15% discount, add-on spend rises with volume [app], recovering part of the $700,000 revenue shortfall [an].

knowledge_max_2: lower prices attract price-sensitive domestic customers
higher occupancy increases ancillary revenue per occupied room
application_max_2: 15% rate cut targets families avoiding the 16% fall in overseas holiday spending
120 rooms at 58% occupancy versus 71% before the slump
analysis_max_2: occupancy recovery towards 71% restores room and add-on revenue
volume gains offset the lower rate per room towards the $700,000 gap

questions.question_text: Do you think Skerry Bay Hotel should cut room rates by 15% rather than close the leisure wing and make 9 staff redundant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting room rates by 15% would win price-sensitive domestic business [k]; with unemployment at 10.2% and holiday spending down 16%, families switching from overseas trips are the realistic growth segment, and rivals have already cut rates by 12% [app], so matching the market could lift occupancy from 58% and protect the $2.4 million revenue base [an]. However, closing the leisure wing and making 9 staff redundant would cut overheads [k]; weak corporate demand (bookings dried up completely) means fixed leisure costs weigh on profit while revenue sits $700,000 below last year's $3.1 million [app], so closure stops losses if the 15% discount fails to fill rooms [an]. Overall, Skerry Bay should cut room rates by 15% [eval], because closing the leisure wing removes the facilities that differentiate the hotel, whereas a targeted discount rebuilds occupancy from 58%, keeps 64 staff in work and preserves the 3-star offer for the recovery [eval].

knowledge_max_2: discounting attracts domestic demand when household budgets are squeezed
closing underused facilities and redundancy cut fixed costs but remove value-adding capacity
application_max_2: 15% rate cut vs rivals already at 12% off and 10.2% unemployment
closing the leisure wing and 9 of 64 staff redundant vs $700,000 revenue shortfall
analysis_max_2: rate cut restores volume and add-on revenue versus deeper margin per room
closure saves costs now but weakens the hotel's offer when demand recovers
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to occupancy of 58% versus 71% before the slump
recommendation keeps facilities and staff for the recovery

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bramwell Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Country X employing 52 workers in one factory, making sofas and dining sets. Country X's economy shows early signs of recovery after 2 quarters of falling GDP: output rose 0.8% last quarter and unemployment edged down from 9.6% to 9.1%. Consumer confidence has improved for 3 consecutive months. Orders climbed from $1.9 million to $2.4 million and lead times shortened from 14 weeks to 11 weeks.

Two national retailers want larger ranges for spring. The owners must decide whether to hire 8 extra production staff and build inventory ahead of the recovery, or to keep staffing at 52 and take orders only as they arrive. Timber prices are 13% higher than two years ago. The board meets in 3 weeks, before the spring retail catalogue deadline.

questions.question_text: Define 'recovery'.
questions.model_answer: The stage of the business cycle when GDP begins to grow again after a recession or slump, and confidence and spending start to rise [2].

knowledge_max_2: the stage when GDP starts to grow after a downturn
confidence and spending begin to rise again

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Bramwell Furniture's order book recovered.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Rising GDP lifts household confidence [k], and with consumer confidence improving for 3 consecutive months and GDP up 0.8%, families are more willing to replace big-ticket furniture [app]. Reason 2: Falling unemployment raises household incomes [k], and with unemployment down from 9.6% to 9.1%, orders climbed from $1.9 million to $2.4 million [app].

knowledge_max_2: recovery raises confidence, encouraging big-ticket spending
falling unemployment increases household disposable income
application_max_2: GDP rose 0.8% and confidence improved for 3 consecutive months
unemployment edged down from 9.6% to 9.1%; orders climbed from $1.9 million to $2.4 million

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bramwell Furniture of hiring 8 extra production staff and building inventory.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Extra staff shorten delivery times [k], letting Bramwell cut lead times from 11 weeks further and satisfy the two national retailers wanting larger ranges for spring [app], winning repeat orders [an]. Benefit 2: Holding inventory ahead of demand captures the early recovery [k], and with the order book already climbing from $1.9 million to $2.4 million, Bramwell can fulfil demand without delays [app], protecting its reputation with national buyers [an].

knowledge_max_2: additional staff reduce lead times and enable larger order fulfilment
holding inventory ahead of demand captures upswing orders
application_max_2: 8 extra staff needed to serve the two national retailers' spring ranges
lead times already shortened from 14 weeks to 11 weeks with orders at $2.4 million
analysis_max_2: shorter lead times win repeat spring orders and strengthen retailer relationships
inventory readiness avoids stockouts and protects revenue during the upswing

questions.question_text: Do you think Bramwell Furniture should hire 8 extra production staff rather than keep staffing at 52? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Hiring 8 extra production staff matches output to the recovery [k]; with GDP up 0.8%, unemployment down to 9.1% and the order book climbing $500,000 to $2.4 million, Bramwell can only cut its 11-week lead times and supply the two national retailers' spring ranges if it lifts capacity [app], so revenue and market share should grow through spring [an]. However, waiting is safer if the recovery stalls [k]; recovery is only early, timber prices are 13% higher than two years ago, and if confidence slips again the extra 8 wages and unsold sofas would squeeze a margin already hit by input costs [app], so keeping staffing at 52 protects cash until orders keep rising [an]. Overall, Bramwell should hire the 8 extra staff [eval], because lead times must fall from 11 weeks to win the two national retailers' spring ranges, and the downside of a modest, reversible staffing increase is smaller than the cost of turning away growing orders [eval].

knowledge_max_2: hiring ahead of recovery wins early market share and retailer listings
holding staffing fixed protects cash if the recovery stalls
application_max_2: 8 extra staff vs keeping 52; order book up $500,000 to $2.4 million
timber prices 13% higher; lead times need to fall from 11 weeks
analysis_max_2: capacity gain versus risk of excess wages if demand softens
winning two national retailers' spring ranges versus cash protection in a fragile recovery
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to the spring retail catalogue deadline in 3 weeks
recommendation weighs the fragile 0.8% GDP recovery against order momentum

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Windlass Recruitment Ltd is a private limited company in Country X placing staff into offices, shops and warehouses. Over the past year, unemployment in Country X fell from 7.8% to 6.4% and advertised vacancies rose 22% to 148,000. Temps charge $28 an hour on average. Windlass filled 2,900 permanent roles and 1,100 temporary posts last year, reaching revenue of $3.7 million, up 13%.

The directors are deciding whether to launch a temporary-staffing division with 6 consultants to meet urgent warehouse demand, or to open a second branch in the industrial north of Country X. A second branch would cost $190,000 to fit out. Temporary demand is forecast to grow 30% next year. The decision must be made within 6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'unemployment'.
questions.model_answer: People of working age who are willing and able to work but cannot find a job, expressed as a percentage of the workforce [2].

knowledge_max_2: people able and willing to work who cannot find jobs
measured as a percentage of the workforce

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of falling unemployment on Windlass Recruitment.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Fewer candidates are available for each vacancy [k], and with unemployment down from 7.8% to 6.4% and vacancies up 22% to 148,000, consultants must search harder to fill the 2,900 permanent roles [app]. Effect 2: Employers compete harder for talent [k], so Windlass must deliver faster shortlists and service to keep its $3.7 million revenue growing at 13% [app].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Cormorant Freight Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating a fleet of 24 trucks from a depot near the motorway, employing 51 staff. Country X's GDP grew 3.1% last year and national freight volumes rose 9%. Fuel costs have steadied after a volatile 2 years. Cormorant's deliveries rose 14% to 38,000 pallets a year, and 3 customers want dedicated daily contracts worth $1.2 million a year that Cormorant cannot cover with current capacity.

The managing director must decide whether to buy 6 new trucks for $780,000 using cash reserves of $900,000, or lease them for 5 years at $9,200 per month per truck. Leased trucks include maintenance and road tax. Buying would lift capacity by 25%. The largest customer signs next quarter.

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Economic growth increases output that must be moved [k], and with GDP up 3.1%, factories and shops need more inbound and outbound transport, lifting national freight volumes by 9% [app]. Reason 2: Growing consumer and business demand raises deliveries [k], which is why Cormorant's own deliveries rose 14% to 38,000 pallets a year [app].

Benefit 2: Owned trucks are reusable assets [k], adding 25% capacity within weeks and full control of use and resale of the 6 trucks [app], strengthening Cormorant's position with the 3 customers [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bluefin Leisure Centres Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating 4 fitness clubs with 21,000 members and 96 staff. After 3 years of growth, Country X's GDP rose just 0.4% last quarter, unemployment crept up from 4.9% to 5.3% and consumer confidence slipped from 112 to 104. Gym visits are down 7% since January.

Membership has plateaued; annual revenue is $8.9 million and costs are rising. Two rival chains have discounted memberships by 20%. The board is deciding whether to press ahead with a 5th premium club in the northern suburbs costing $3.6 million, signed this quarter, or to freeze expansion, cut costs by $600,000 a year and prepare for a possible downturn. The 5th club would create 30 jobs. The decision is due within 4 weeks.

questions.model_answer: The recurring pattern of growth and decline in an economy, moving through boom, recession, slump and recovery [2].

questions.model_answer: Sign 1: GDP growth has slowed sharply [k], and after 3 years of growth output rose just 0.4% last quarter, signalling that momentum is fading [app]. Sign 2: Confidence and unemployment are turning [k], with confidence slipping from 112 to 104 and unemployment creeping up from 4.9% to 5.3%, both classic late-cycle warnings [app].

falling confidence and rising unemployment are late-cycle signals
application_max_2: GDP rose just 0.4% last quarter after 3 years of growth

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bluefin of pressing ahead with the 5th premium club.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A first mover captures the northern suburbs [k], winning demand before rivals react as the premium club creates 30 jobs and lifts capacity beyond 21,000 members [app], securing revenue through the plateau [an]. Benefit 2: Fitness demand often holds up early in a slowdown [k], and with revenue at $8.9 million across 4 clubs, a premium site could lift yield per member [app], diversifying income across locations [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Bluefin Leisure Centres should press ahead with the 5th premium club rather than freeze expansion? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Pressing ahead captures remaining growth before the cycle turns [k]; GDP rose 0.4% last quarter and confidence still stands at 104, so northern-suburb demand may absorb a premium club creating 30 jobs, lifting capacity beyond 21,000 members and revenue above $8.9 million [app], so Bluefin would enter any downturn as the larger, stronger operator [an]. However, freezing expansion is the prudent response to clear late-cycle signals [k]; with growth of just 0.4%, unemployment rising to 5.3%, confidence slipping from 112 to 104 and two rivals discounting memberships by 20%, a $3.6 million commitment could strain Bluefin if member numbers fall [app], whereas cutting costs by $600,000 a year shields margins through a downturn [an]. Overall, Bluefin should freeze expansion for now [eval], because the late-cycle data (0.4% GDP, confidence 104, rivals discounting 20%) outweigh the case for a $3.6 million club, and the northern suburbs can be entered once confidence stabilises [eval].
